plain: JavaScript is the language almost every website is written in. For years only the browser understood it, meaning the program you use to view web pages, like Chrome. Node.js is an interpreter you install on your computer so it understands that same language without opening any browser. It's like going from having to visit the embassy every time you need a document translated to having the translator living in your living room: the language is the same, what changes is that it now works at home, any time of day.

account.free: Node.js and npm are free and open source. Zero dollars, always. No account, no email, no card, no hidden paid plan. One thing to watch out for: Node is free, but what you install with it might not be. Claude Code needs a Claude subscription, around $17-20 a month for the Pro plan, or pay-per-use. n8n installed on your own computer is free; its cloud-hosted version starts around $20-24 a month.
steps: Type nodejs.org into your browser. It doesn't ask you to register or leave your email: the download starts right away. In the middle of the page there's a big button that says Download Node.js (LTS), meaning download the long-term-support version.

The site offers you two versions. LTS is the stable one, the one millions of people have been using for months. Current is the freshly released one, with new features and bugs. For everything you'll do in this course, LTS. As of writing this is the 24 series, so you'll see something like 24.x.x.
Download the installer for your system

The page detects whether you're on Windows or Mac and gives you the right file. On Windows it's a .msi file of about 30 MB. On Mac it's a .pkg. If your Mac has an Apple chip (M1, M2, M3, or M4) choose the ARM64 option; if it's an older Intel Mac, choose x64.
Run the installer and don't touch anything odd

Double-click the downloaded file. The license screen appears, check I accept the terms, and keep clicking Next until Install. Leave the Add to PATH checkbox checked: it's what lets your computer know where to find Node from any folder. If you uncheck it, nothing that comes after will work.

Near the end, the Windows installer offers a checkbox that says Automatically install the necessary tools. Leave it UNCHECKED. If you check it, a black window opens and spends twenty minutes downloading several gigabytes of compilers you're not going to use.

Open the terminal, which is the window where you type commands as text instead of clicking: on Windows it's called PowerShell, on Mac it's called Terminal. Type node -v and press Enter. It should respond with something like v24.4.1. Now type npm -v and it should respond with another number, like 11.3.0. If it says it doesn't recognize the command, close that window and open it again: the terminal only checks the list of programs when it starts up.

With the terminal open, type npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code and press Enter. It takes one to three minutes and floods the screen with lots of text; that's normal, not an error. When it's done, type claude and you'll have Claude Code running. You've just used Node without writing a single line of programming.
account.warning: Every time you type npm install something, your computer downloads code written by a stranger and runs it with your permissions: it can read your files and your saved passwords. This isn't paranoia, it has actually happened: a package called crossenv, copying the name of the legitimate cross-env, stole data from anyone who mistyped it. Always copy the exact name from the tool's official documentation, never from a forum comment. And if you're on a Mac, never put sudo in front of npm install: it installs things as an administrator and undoing it means deleting system folders by hand, exactly the kind of afternoon you don't want to have.

first: Open the terminal and type node -v. Seeing the version number appear is your confirmation that it exists.
Create a new folder called test on the Desktop and enter it from the terminal with cd Desktop/test.
Type npm init -y. In half a second a file called package.json appears. Open it with Notepad: it's ten lines, and all of them are understandable.
Type npm install dayjs. Look at what changed: a node_modules folder appeared, a package-lock.json file appeared, and there's a new line inside package.json with dayjs. That's the whole mechanism.
Type npx cowsay hello. A drawn cow shows up saying hello, and you haven't installed anything permanent. You've just seen the difference between npm and npx.
words: The program you install so your computer can understand on its own the language web pages are written in. Without it, that language only works inside the browser.
Short for Node Package Manager. It's two things at once: a public warehouse with more than three million packages, and the command you type to fetch them.
A chunk of work already done by someone else and packaged for you to use without writing it yourself. Claude Code is a package. n8n is a package. That's why both are installed the same way.
A short text file that's your project's ID card: what it's called, what version it's on, and the list of packages it needs. If you keep that file, anyone can rebuild the whole project from scratch.
The folder where all the packages you've downloaded land. It's huge, has thousands of subfolders, and is disposable: it can be deleted and refilled with a single command.
The command for using something once without leaving it installed on your computer. It fetches it, runs it in front of you, and throws it away.
Those two letters make whatever you fetch available across the whole computer, not just the folder you were in. It's what turns claude or n8n into a word you can type from anywhere.
Long Term Support. The boring version, the one millions of people have been using for months and no longer gives surprises. It's the one you want.
matters: Install the LTS version and not Current. n8n and Claude Code state which versions they work with, and one that's too new fails with long, unreadable error messages that will make you think the tool is broken when the problem is yours and takes a minute to fix.

The installer's Add to PATH checkbox, and closing and reopening the terminal afterward. Skip either one and your computer will tell you it doesn't recognize the node command even though Node is perfectly installed. It's the number one error of the first few days, and people spend two hours uninstalling and reinstalling for nothing.

Notice which folder you're in before typing npm install. npm always works on the folder you're currently in. If you type it while on the Desktop, it creates a node_modules folder there with thousands of files that you then don't know if you can delete.

Tell apart installing inside a project from installing for the whole computer. Tools you want to be able to call from anywhere, like Claude Code or n8n, take -g. Packages used by just one specific project go without -g. Confusing the two produces the classic, maddening 'it works in one folder and not in the other'.
ignore: What's inside node_modules and the ten thousand lines of package-lock.json. Neither is meant to be read: they're the equivalent of the engine and the itemized shopping list. Your work is with package.json, which does fit on one screen.

Learning to write JavaScript. You install Node so you can use tools other people have already written, the same way you install a PDF reader without knowing how to build PDFs. If you ever want to write code, that's a separate decision, not a requirement to get started today.

The npm vs. yarn vs. pnpm debate you'll see in tutorials and on Reddit. They're three ways of doing exactly the same thing. npm already comes bundled with Node and lacks nothing for what you need; the other two solve problems for large, fast-moving teams.

questions.prompt: You want to try n8n. You search Google, find a blog post that says npm install n8n, run it inside your Documents folder, and everything seems fine: two minutes of text and no red errors. Then you type n8n to start it up and the terminal says it doesn't recognize the command. You check node -v and it responds with v24.4.1, no problem.

options.text: You installed it only for that folder. To be able to call it from anywhere, you need npm install -g n8n, with the -g for global.
options.why: Correct, and the nuance is in the detail that node -v does respond: that proves Node is set up correctly and the problem is only where n8n lives. Without -g, the tool exists, but only inside the Documents folder and only if you call it from inside that folder with npx n8n. The -g puts it in the spot on the computer where the terminal looks for commands.

options.text: Node is badly installed. You need to uninstall it, restart the computer, and start over with the installer from scratch.
options.why: It really does get believed, because the message you see, command not recognized, is word for word the same one that shows up when Node is badly installed, so the instinct is to blame the foundation. But it breaks at a specific point: node -v just responded with its version. If Node were badly installed, that command would have failed too. Uninstalling and reinstalling would cost you half an hour and leave you in exactly the same spot.

options.text: A step is missing: you have to type npm start inside the folder to start it up.
options.why: It's reasonable because in a great many tutorials the step after installing really is npm start, so the sequence sounds familiar. Where it breaks: npm start only works if that folder has a package.json with a start script defined saying what to run. Your Documents folder doesn't have one, so npm start would answer with a different error and you'd be equally stuck.

questions.explain: Without -g, a package only exists inside the exact folder where you installed it.

questions.prompt: You're following a tutorial to set up the skeleton of a website, and the first step asks you to type npx create-next-app my-site. You hesitate: you haven't installed anything called create-next-app and you're worried it'll fail halfway and leave your computer in a half-done state.

options.text: Type it as it is. npx downloads the tool, runs it, and doesn't leave it installed on your computer.
options.why: Correct, and the nuance that makes it correct is the purpose: create-next-app is a tool you use once and won't touch again for months. npx exists exactly for that, so you don't clutter your computer with one-off things. And since it's downloaded on the spot, you always get today's version instead of one frozen eight months ago.

options.text: No, first you need to run npm install -g create-next-app. npx only works for launching things that are already installed.
options.why: It's believed because it was literally true before 2017, and there are thousands of old tutorials that still explain it that way. It breaks halfway: npx does run what you already have if it finds it, but if it doesn't find it, it downloads it on its own, which is the case here. Also, installing it with -g has a real cost: it leaves you a frozen version that, six months from now, will keep generating outdated projects without telling you.

options.text: npx and npm are the same thing written two different ways, you can use either one.
options.why: It's an honest mix-up: they differ by one letter, come in the same installer, and appear mixed together on the same documentation page. But they do opposite things: npm saves, npx runs. If you type npm create-next-app my-site you'll get an error, because npm expects one of its own commands after it, like install, init, or run, not the name of a tool.

questions.explain: npm saves forever, npx uses and throws away.

shortcuts: node -v and npm -v

The first two commands you always type. They return a version number, for example v20.11.0 and 10.2.4. If instead of a number you get 'the term is not recognized', it's either not installed or the terminal was opened before it was installed. This is the check to make before writing to anyone asking for help.
npm install (or npm i, same thing)

With nothing after it, it reads the package.json of the folder you're in and downloads everything that project needs. It's the command you type when you download a project from the internet. With a name after it (npm install dayjs) it adds a new package to that project.
npm run <name>

Runs one of the shortcuts a project has defined in package.json, under scripts. The three names you'll always see: dev (start it on your computer to work on it), build (prepare it for publishing), and start (start it as if it were the real server). If you don't remember which ones exist, type npm run by itself and it'll list them.
npx <tool>

Runs a tool WITHOUT installing it permanently: it downloads it, uses it, and throws it away. It's what's behind those tutorial commands like npx create-next-app. Use it for one-off things; save npm install -g for what you use every day.
npm install -g <tool>

The -g means global: it installs it for the whole computer, not for one project. This is how you install tools you want to be able to call from anywhere, like Claude Code. Rule: global only for tools; never for a project's own pieces.
cd and the line where the terminal starts

cd means 'enter a folder' (cd my-project) and cd .. means 'go up one level'. Before typing anything with npm, look at what's shown at the start of the line: that's the folder it's going to act on. Almost every beginner disaster is a correct command typed in the wrong folder.
Ctrl+C in the terminal

Stops whatever's running. When you start something with npm run dev, the terminal stays busy and stops accepting commands: it's not frozen, it's working. Ctrl+C stops it and gives you the line back. It means 'stop', not 'copy'.
npm outdated and npm update

The first lists which of your project's packages have a newer version, without touching anything. The second updates them within safe margins. While you're learning, check the first one now and then, and don't run the second if the project is working: updating for sport breaks more than it fixes.
npm ls <package> and npm why <package>

When something breaks and you don't know where a package came from, these two tell you what version you have installed and who brought it in. Mostly useful for pasting the answer to the AI when it asks 'what version of this do you have?'.
The terminal's trash icon, not the X

In the editor, the X hides the terminal but leaves the process running behind it. The trash icon actually kills it. It explains that common 'port 3000 is already in use' error: your project is running in a terminal you thought was closed.
daily: Install the LTS version and no other. LTS means long-term support and stability. The tools you're going to use (Claude Code, n8n, web projects) state which versions they work with, and the Current version, the newest one, breaks things without warning. If you've already installed it and something's failing oddly, uninstall it and put LTS in.

Understand what each file that appears on its own is. package.json is the project's shopping list: what packages it needs and what shortcuts it has. package-lock.json is the receipt with the exact versions that got downloaded; it gets uploaded to the internet and never edited by hand. node_modules is the pantry with the downloaded packages: it weighs hundreds of megabytes and NEVER gets uploaded.

Never upload node_modules. It has to be in .gitignore. If you upload it, the project becomes absurdly heavy and gives errors on the next computer over. And if that folder is missing, don't ask for it: it regenerates by typing npm install.

Delete and rebuild before investigating. When a project that was working starts giving incoherent errors while installing, delete the node_modules folder and the package-lock.json file, and type npm install again. It sounds brutal and fixes half of all cases in two minutes.

Read the first two lines of the error, not the forty. npm spits out walls of text. What matters is at the top: a line starting with npm ERR! code and another naming the package. That's what to copy; the rest is filler.

Tell a warning apart from an error. When installing, yellow 'deprecated' notices and vulnerability warnings show up almost every time. If it ends with 'added 250 packages', it worked. Don't run npm audit fix --force to clear the warnings: that command changes versions aggressively and is a classic way to break a project that was working fine.
One project, one folder, one terminal. When working with two projects at once, open two editor windows. Mixing folders in the same terminal ends with packages installed in the wrong place.

templates.name: The minimal package.json you can read start to finish
templates.what: It's your project's ID card: what it's called, what commands it has, and what packages it needs. When the AI tells you 'run npm run dev', this is what makes that command possible. Worth reading through slowly once, because it's ten lines and explains 80% of what happens afterward.
templates.how: 1) Create a folder with a short name, lowercase, no spaces. 2) Enter it from the terminal with cd. 3) Type npm init -y to have it created automatically. 4) Open it and compare it with the one below. 5) Add the scripts section by hand with whatever shortcuts you want. 6) From then on, every npm install you run will note itself under dependencies automatically.
fill: name
The project's name, lowercase, no spaces or accents. Can't start with a dot or an underscore
type
module lets you use the modern way of writing (import). If a tutorial uses require, remove this line
engines
The Node version you know it works with. It's a warning for you and for anyone who opens it on another computer
scripts.dev
The shortcut for working on your computer. This is the one you'll use every day
scripts.start
How it actually starts up for real. This is what the server will run once you publish it
dependencies
The packages the project needs to work. This fills itself in via npm install

templates.name: The first file that actually does something, with keys kept out of the code
templates.what: A twenty-line file that reads a secret key from outside the code, checks it exists, and warns you in plain English if it's missing. It's the pattern that repeats in everything you'll build afterward: a password never gets written inside a file that gets uploaded to the internet.
templates.how: 1) Create index.js with this content. 2) Create .env.local with your real key. 3) Create .gitignore with the line .env*.local inside it. 4) Type node --env-file=.env.local index.js. 5) If the red warning shows up, the key isn't getting through: check the name, it needs to be written exactly the same in both places. Note: --env-file needs Node 20 or newer; if you have less, update to LTS.
fill: OPENAI_API_KEY
The key's name. It has to be written EXACTLY the same in .env.local and in the code, capitalization included
process.env
The keychain Node reads from outside the code. Everything here comes from .env.local, never from the file itself
--env-file
The modern way to load the keys file without installing anything. Needs Node 20 or newer
.gitignore
Without the .env*.local line inside it, your key ends up published the first time you upload the project

errors: 'node' is not recognized as an internal or external command

Either it's not installed, or it's installed but this terminal was opened before that and doesn't know it. Try the free option first: close the whole terminal (and the editor too if you use it from there) and open it again. If it's still the same, reinstall from nodejs.org choosing LTS and making sure to leave the 'Add to PATH' checkbox checked. On Mac with Homebrew: brew install node@20.
npm ERR! code ENOENT · no such file or directory, open 'package.json'

Translation: 'there's no project here'. You're typing an npm command in a folder that has no package.json, almost always because you're one level above or below the project. Check the terminal's line to see where you are, cd into the right folder, and confirm with dir (Windows) or ls (Mac) that you see package.json before repeating the command.
npm ERR! code EACCES · permission denied

The system won't let you write where npm wants to write. Shows up almost always on Mac or Linux when using npm install -g. Do NOT fix it by putting sudo in front: that leaves files with the wrong owner and will cause worse problems a month from now. The clean fix is installing Node with nvm (a version manager), which puts it inside your user folder and makes the problem disappear for good.
npm ERR! code ERESOLVE · unable to resolve dependency tree

Two pieces of your project are asking for incompatible versions of a third one. Shows up a lot when following old tutorials. First, delete node_modules and package-lock.json and try npm install again. If it persists, paste the whole error to the AI and ask it to tell you which two packages are clashing and what specific version to pin. The npm install --force the error itself suggests will install something broken anyway: only use it if you understand what you're forcing.
Error: listen EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000

Port 3000 is already being used by another program: almost always your own project, running in a terminal you thought was closed. Fix it: find that terminal and press Ctrl+C. If you can't find it, on Windows type npx kill-port 3000 and on Mac lsof -ti:3000 | xargs kill. The lazy alternative is starting on a different port, but you'll end up with five zombie projects.
Warning: To load an ES module, set "type": "module" in the package.json

There are two ways to write JavaScript, the old one (require) and the modern one (import), and your file uses one while the project is set up for the other. Fix it in a second: add the line "type": "module" in package.json if your code uses import, or remove it if it uses require. Don't mix the two in the same project.
found 12 vulnerabilities (3 moderate, 9 high) · run npm audit fix

It's a warning, not an error, and shows up almost every time. It means some distant package has a known flaw. While you're still learning on your own computer, ignore it: don't run npm audit fix --force, because that command changes versions aggressively and is the classic way to break a project that was working. Once the project is real and published, that's when it's worth reviewing carefully.
Node.js version X is not supported / requires Node >= 20

The tool you're trying to use needs a newer version than what you have. Check with node -v and update to LTS from nodejs.org. If you need several versions at once because an old project won't run on the new one, install nvm: it lets you switch versions by typing one line, without uninstalling anything.

prompts.name: Check that my computer is ready before I start
prompts.prompt: Act as the technical person walking me through this. I don't know how to code and I'm not going to learn: I'll type what you tell me and paste back what comes out. I want to check that my computer is ready to work with Node.js projects before starting anything, because I'd rather find out now what's missing than in the middle of a tutorial. Do it like this. One: give me, one at a time, the commands I need to type in the terminal to check what I have installed (Node, npm, Git, and whatever else you think matters), and after each one tell me which response means 'good', which means 'you have it but it's old', and which means 'you don't have it'. Two: wait for me to paste the responses before continuing. Three: once I paste them, give me a table of what's fine, what needs updating, and what's missing, ordered by what's going to cause problems soonest. Four: for everything that needs installing or updating, tell me where to download it (exact address), which specific version to choose and why that one and not the newest, and which installer checkboxes I absolutely must check. Five: warn me about any step where I need to close and reopen the terminal, because I always forget that and then think it didn't work. I'm on [WINDOWS / MAC] and what I want to end up using is: [CLAUDE CODE / N8N / A WEBSITE / WHATEVER APPLIES].

prompts.name: Get a project I downloaded running when it won't start
prompts.prompt: I downloaded a project from the internet and can't get it to start. I don't know how to code: tell me exactly what to type, in what order, and what should show up each time. Before suggesting anything, ask me for what you need to see: the contents of package.json, the response to node -v and npm -v, and the list of files in the folder. Don't guess. Once you have that, answer me like this. One: what this project is and what it needs to work, in two sentences. Two: the exact list of commands to type, one at a time, each with what should show up if it goes well. Three: tell me whether it needs a keys file (.env or similar) and, if so, what those keys are, where to get each one, and what happens if I start it without them. Four: tell me what browser address to open it at once it starts, and how to stop it when I'm done. Five: if at some point something fails, I want you to first tell me how to tell an unimportant warning apart from a real error, because in the terminal it all shows up together and in red. Six: at the end, tell me the single command I need to type tomorrow to start it again. The project is: [WHERE YOU GOT IT FROM AND WHAT IT'S SUPPOSED TO DO].

prompts.name: Translate an npm error I don't understand
prompts.prompt: An npm command failed on me and spat out forty lines in red. I'm pasting them all below. I don't know how to code, so I need the following, in this order, no theory. One: tell me which of those lines actually matter and which are filler, pointing them out, because I want to learn to read them myself next time. Two: what happened, in one sentence of plain English. Three: whether I broke this myself, whether it's a version mismatch between pieces of the project, whether something's missing that needs installing, or whether I'm in the wrong folder. Four: the solution in numbered steps, always starting with the least aggressive option; if the solution involves deleting node_modules and package-lock.json, tell me clearly and explain what's lost by deleting them (spoiler: nothing, I want that confirmed). Five: tell me explicitly whether any of the solutions floating around out there (npm install --force, npm audit fix --force, putting sudo in front) is a bad idea in my case and why, because I'm going to run into them in forums. Six: how I avoid this happening again. I'm on [WINDOWS / MAC], my version is [PASTE THE node -v RESPONSE], I was trying to [WHAT YOU WERE DOING], and the error is: [PASTE THE WHOLE ERROR].

prompts.name: Decide whether to install something inside the project or for the whole computer
prompts.prompt: I'm going to install things with npm and I don't want to end up with my computer full of junk or with projects that only work on my machine. I'll tell you what I want to install and I need you to decide for me and justify it. For each thing, answer me: one, whether it goes inside the project (npm install) or for the whole computer (npm install -g), and why that one and not the other; two, the exact command to type and which folder I need to be in when I type it; three, which files in my project will change after installing it and whether any of them should or shouldn't be uploaded to the internet; four, roughly how much space it takes and whether it has any known gotcha; five, how to uninstall it if I change my mind. Also, before giving me anything: tell me if any of the things I've asked for actually aren't needed because they already come bundled with something else, or because there's a way to use it without installing anything, via npx. I'd rather install three things I understand than ten I don't. What I want to install is: [LIST OF THINGS]. My project is: [DESCRIBE IT IN ONE SENTENCE].
